93-r1.sourceTitle: Čech cohomology and de Rham's theorem: class lecture for Math 758, Spring 2008
93-r1.locator: Joshua P. Bowman, Example 2.6 (Poincaré lemma gives an exact sequence of sheaves), Def. 4.1, Example 4.2, Lemma 4.3 (fine sheaves have no higher cohomology via partitions of unity), Cor. 5.2 and Theorem 5.3 (de Rham's theorem), pp. 3, 5-6, 8
93-r1.proofSketch: Consider the complex of sheaves $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$. The Poincaré lemma says closed forms are locally exact, so this sequence of sheaves is exact. Each $\Omega^k_M$ is fine, because local sections can be glued by a partition of unity (multiply by the partition functions and sum), and a fine sheaf has vanishing higher Čech cohomology by an explicit homotopy built from the partition of unity. Hence the sequence is a fine resolution of the constant sheaf, and the cohomology of its global sections, namely de Rham cohomology, equals the Čech (sheaf) cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$.

93-r3.sourceTitle: Čech cohomology and de Rham's theorem: class lecture for Math 758, Spring 2008
93-r3.locator: Joshua P. Bowman, Def. 4.4 (fine resolution), Theorem 4.5, Corollaries 5.1-5.2 and Theorem 5.3 (de Rham's theorem), pp. 6-8
93-r3.proofSketch: Define a fine resolution of a sheaf $\mathcal F$ as an exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F^0\to\mathcal F^1\to\cdots$ with every $\mathcal F^k$ fine. Theorem 4.5 compares the Čech cohomology of a good cover with the cohomology of the complex of global sections of the resolution by chasing a double complex: rows below the first are exact because the $\mathcal F^k$ are fine, columns are exact by the hypothesis on the cover. Passing to the limit over covers (Leray) gives that the cohomology of $\mathcal F$ equals that of the global sections complex of any fine resolution. Applied to $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\to\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$, a fine resolution by the Poincaré lemma and partitions of unity, this identifies sheaf cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$ with de Rham cohomology.

93-r2.locator: Lily Li, Section 3, Definition 3.1 and Theorem 3.5 (De Rham Theorem) with proof, pp. 9-10
93-r2.proofSketch: Call a manifold de Rham if the integration map $H^p_{dR}(M)\to H^p(M;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism, and a cover a de Rham cover if its members and all their finite intersections are de Rham. Disjoint unions of de Rham manifolds are de Rham, and convex open sets in $\mathbb R^n$ are de Rham by the Poincaré lemma and homotopy invariance. For a finite de Rham cover, induct on the number of sets: compare the Mayer-Vietoris sequences of de Rham and singular cohomology for $U=U_1\cup\dots\cup U_k$ and $V=U_{k+1}$, and conclude with the five lemma. For a de Rham basis, an exhaustion function splits $M$ into two disjoint unions of finitely covered pieces, whose union and intersection are de Rham. Open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, hence every manifold, have such a basis of balls.

94-r1.proofSketch: Use Cartan's formula $L_\xi=d\,i(\xi)+i(\xi)d$. For a family of maps $f_t$ with velocity field $\xi_t$, differentiate $f_t^*\omega$ to get $\frac{d}{dt}f_t^*\omega=f_t^*L_{\xi_t}\omega$. Integrate over $t\in[0,1]$ and apply Cartan's formula to obtain $f_1^*\omega-f_0^*\omega=dJ\omega+Jd\omega$ with $J\omega=\int_0^1 f_t^*i(\xi_t)\omega\,dt$. On a ball centred at $x_0$ take the radial contraction $f_t(x)=t(x-x_0)+x_0$, so $f_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $f_0^*\omega=0$ for forms of positive degree; hence $\omega=dJ\omega$ when $d\omega=0$.

94-r2.proofSketch: For a star-shaped open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ consider forms on $U\times[0,1]$ and define fiber integration $\pi_*$ by integrating the coefficient of $dt$ over $[0,1]$. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\pi_*(d\alpha)=\alpha_1-\alpha_0-d(\pi_*\alpha)$. Pull back along the straight-line contraction $h(x,t)=tx$ and set $J=\pi_*\circ h^*$ to obtain the homotopy formula $h_1^*\omega-h_0^*\omega=Jd\omega+dJ\omega$. For closed $\omega$ of positive degree, $h_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $h_0^*\omega=0$, so $\omega=dJ\omega$.

94-r3.locator: Lead section, paragraph on cohomology ('In the language of cohomology ...')
94-r3.proofSketch: The route proposes deducing local exactness from vanishing of reduced singular cohomology of a contractible set and the de Rham theorem. The cited article states that the vanishing of singular cohomology of a contractible space does not give the Poincare lemma, because the de Rham theorem (singular = de Rham cohomology) itself relies on the Poincare lemma. The route is therefore circular as a proof of the lemma; it is only valid as a consistency check once the de Rham theorem is known by independent means.

94-r3.transcriptionNotes: No proof exists in the source for this route; the source only remarks on its circularity. Li's De Rham Cohomology (Thm 3.5) likewise uses the Poincare lemma to prove the de Rham theorem.
94-r3.reasonNotReproduced: No source proves the lemma by this route; Wikipedia explicitly notes the de Rham theorem relies on the Poincare lemma, making the route circular.

95-r1.locator: Section 'Symmetric version' and 'Proof of the symmetric form of Rouché's theorem'
95-r1.proofSketch: The symmetric strict inequality $|f-g|<|f|+|g|$ on $\partial K$ implies $f,g$ have no zeros there and $g$ is never a negative real multiple of $f$. By the argument principle $N_f(K)$ equals the winding number of $f\circ C$ about $0$, and likewise for $g$. The segment homotopy $H_t=(1-t)f\circ C+t\,g\circ C$ avoids the origin, and the winding number $I(t)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{H_t}dz/z$ is continuous and integer-valued, hence constant. So $N_f(K)=N_g(K)$. The usual form $|g|<|f|$ follows by applying this to $f+g$ and $f$.

95-r2.locator: Section 'Proof of the symmetric form of Rouché's theorem' (argument principle step) with preceding 'Symmetric version'
95-r2.proofSketch: Apply the argument principle: since $f$ has no zeros on the boundary curve $C$, $N_f(K)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C f'/f\,dz$, which equals the winding number of $f\circ C$ about $0$; the same holds for $g$. Because the hypothesis keeps the segment between $f(C(x))$ and $g(C(x))$ away from $0$, the family $H_t$ of curves has constant (integer-valued, continuous) winding number in $t$. Hence the winding numbers of $f\circ C$ and $g\circ C$, and so the zero counts, coincide.

95-r2.transcriptionNotes: Same excerpt as 95-r1: the single proof uses the argument principle and homotopy invariance together. The stored sketch for this route phrases it with $f'/f$ and $(f+g)'/(f+g)$; the source uses $f$ and $g$ in the symmetric form.

95-r3.proofSketch: The theorem is used by writing a function as a dominating part plus a perturbation: if $|g|<|f|$ on $\partial K$ then $f$ and $f+g$ have the same number of zeros in $K$ (for instance $z^5+3z^3+7$ has five zeros in $|z|<2$ because $|3z^3+7|\le31<32=|z^5|$ there). The informal explanation: with $h=f+g$ the condition says $f(z)$ is closer to $h(z)$ than to the origin all along $C$, so the two image curves wind around the origin the same number of times and the argument principle gives equal zero counts.
